pages.summary: An ARIMA model of a time series: autoregressive, integrated, moving average.
body: y(t) depends on its own past (AR, p lags), on past innovations (MA, q lags), after differencing D times; seasonal terms (SAR, SMA at their actual lags, 12 not 1) and predictors (`Beta`, an ARIMAX model) can be added, and the innovations' variance can be a constant or a `garch`, `egarch` or `gjr` model. Parameters given as NaN are what `estimate` fits; numbers are held. AR, MA, SAR and SMA are cells of coefficients, a 0 leaving a lag out. `P` is the whole AR degree, differences included.
syntax: A model whose parameters are to be estimated.
Lags of one's choosing, seasonal terms.

pages.summary: Conditional variance models: the variance of the innovations changing with their recent size.
body: GARCH: v(t) = Constant + Σ GARCH(i) v(t-i) + Σ ARCH(j) e(t-j)², where e(t) = y(t) - Offset; the variance is persistent when the GARCH and ARCH coefficients sum near 1. EGARCH models log v(t), with `Leverage` terms in the standardized innovations z = e/√v so that falls and rises can weigh differently; GJR adds Leverage(j) e(t-j)² where e(t-j) < 0, so that negative innovations weigh more. NaN parameters are estimated.

pages.summary: A vector autoregression: several series, each depending on the past of all of them.
body: y(t) = Constant + Trend t + AR{1} y(t-1) + ... + AR{p} y(t-p) + Beta x(t) + e(t), the innovations e with covariance `Covariance`. NaN values are what `estimate` fits (by least squares, the likelihood's maximum).
syntax: With lags, a trend and predictors.

pages.summary: A model's NaN parameters estimated by maximum likelihood, and the fit summarized.
body: For `arima`, the first P observations are the presample unless `'Y0'` is given, and presample innovations are 0 (or `'E0'`); predictors come as `'X'`. For `garch`, `egarch` and `gjr`, y holds the innovations themselves. `varm` is fitted by least squares, its covariance the residuals' (divided by T). The outputs are the fitted model, the estimates' covariance (or standard errors for varm), the log-likelihood and more. `summarize` shows the estimates with their standard errors, t statistics and p-values, the sample size, the log-likelihood, AIC and BIC, or gives them as a struct.
syntax: [EstMdl, EstParamCov, logL, info] = estimate(Mdl, y, 'Y0', y0, 'X', X, 'Display', 'off')
With the estimates' covariance and the log-likelihood.
The estimates and the fit shown.

pages.summary: Forecasts of a model, sample paths of it, and the innovations it implies for data.
body: `forecast` gives minimum mean square error forecasts from the presample Y0 (at least P values; a column for each path), with their mean square errors, which grow with the model's moving-average weights; a variance model forecasts the conditional variances. `simulate` draws paths from the language's random number generator, the presample at the model's mean unless given. `infer` gives the innovations (residuals) a model implies for data, their variances and the log-likelihood.
syntax: Forecasts and their mean square errors.
Sample paths, their innovations and variances.

pages.summary: The impulse response of a dynamic system, or of an ARIMA model.
body: For a system (`tf`, `ss`, `zpk`): its response to a unit impulse, drawn without outputs. For an `arima` model: the weights of its infinite moving-average form, 1 first, how a single innovation is felt later (a stem plot without outputs).

examples.title: An ARMA(1,1) model's weights
examples.intro: For y(t) = 0.5 y(t-1) + e(t) + 0.4 e(t-1) the weights are 1, then 0.9 0.5^(k-1).

pages.summary: A vector autoregression's impulse responses and forecast error variance decomposition.
body: `irf` gives Response(t, j, k), variable k's response at time t-1 to a shock of one standard deviation to variable j: orthogonalized by the Cholesky factor of the covariance (the default, which depends on the order of the series) or `'generalized'`. `fevd` gives Decomposition(t, j, k), the share of variable k's forecast error variance at horizon t due to shocks to variable j; each row's shares sum to 1. Without outputs `irf` draws the responses.

examples.title: Who moves whom

pages.summary: Sample autocorrelations, partial autocorrelations and cross-correlations, with bounds.
body: `autocorr` gives the correlation of the series with itself k steps back, lags 0 to k (min(20, n-1)), with bounds of ±2 standard errors (`'NumSTD'`) by Bartlett's formula for an MA(q) process (`'NumMA'`, 0: white noise). `parcorr` gives the partial autocorrelations, the last coefficient of y regressed on its first m lags (`'ols'`, or `'yule-walker'`), with bounds ±s/√n past lag p. `crosscorr` gives the correlation of y1(t+k) with y2(t), for lags -k to k. Without outputs, each draws stems with the bounds. An AR(p) process's partial autocorrelations stop after lag p; an MA(q)'s autocorrelations after lag q.
syntax: [acf, lags, bounds] = autocorr(y, 'NumLags', k, 'NumMA', q, 'NumSTD', s)
[pacf, lags, bounds] = parcorr(y, 'NumLags', k, 'NumAR', p, 'Method', m)

pages.summary: Tests of a unit root, and of stationarity.
body: `adftest` (augmented Dickey-Fuller) regresses the differences on the lagged level and lagged differences: h = true rejects a unit root. Its model is `'AR'` (no constant, the default), `'ARD'` (with a drift) or `'TS'` (trend stationary); its statistic `'t1'`, `'t2'` or `'F'`. `pptest` (Phillips-Perron) uses the regression without lagged differences and corrects its statistics for autocorrelation with a Newey-West variance. `kpsstest` turns the question round: its null is stationarity (about a trend, or a level), and h = true rejects it; with autocorrelated data it needs lags, or it rejects too often. Options given as vectors run a test for each.
syntax: [h, pValue, stat, cValue, reg] = adftest(y, 'model', m, 'lags', k, 'test', t, 'alpha', a)
[h, pValue, stat, cValue, reg] = pptest(y, 'model', m, 'lags', k)
[h, pValue, stat, cValue] = kpsstest(y, 'lags', k, 'trend', tf)

pages.summary: Tests of residuals: autocorrelation (Ljung-Box) and conditional heteroscedasticity (Engle's ARCH test).
body: `lbqtest` sums the squared autocorrelations, Q = n(n+2) Σ r_k²/(n-k), up to `'Lags'`, chi-square with `'DOF'` degrees of freedom (Lags unless given: take off a fitted model's parameters for its residuals). `archtest` regresses the squared residuals on their lags: T R², chi-square with Lags degrees of freedom. h = true rejects white noise, or constant variance.
syntax: [h, pValue, stat, cValue] = lbqtest(res, 'Lags', k, 'DOF', d)

pages.summary: The variance ratio test of a random walk.
body: y holds log prices. The variance of q-period returns over q times the variance of one-period returns (Lo and MacKinlay) is 1 for a random walk; above 1 means trends, below 1 reversion. The test is robust to heteroscedasticity unless `'IID'` is true; h = true rejects the random walk.
syntax: [h, pValue, stat, cValue, ratio] = vratiotest(y, 'period', q, 'IID', tf, 'alpha', a)

examples.title: A random walk, and one whose returns persist

pages.summary: The Engle-Granger test of cointegration: whether series that wander share a common trend.
body: The first column is regressed on the others (with a constant `'c'`, none `'nc'`, a trend `'ct'` or a quadratic trend `'ctt'`), then a Dickey-Fuller test of the residuals: if they are stationary, the series are cointegrated. h = true rejects no cointegration. Up to 6 series.
syntax: [h, pValue, stat, cValue, reg] = egcitest(Y, 'creg', c, 'lags', k, 'alpha', a)
The test, and the cointegrating regression.

examples.title: Two series tied together, and two apart

pages.summary: Comparing fitted models: information criteria, and likelihood ratio, Wald and Lagrange multiplier tests.
body: `aicbic` gives AIC = -2 logL + 2k and BIC = -2 logL + k log(n) (and AICc, CAIC and HQC in its third output), smaller being better. The three tests ask whether restrictions on the parameters hold: `lratiotest` from both models' log-likelihoods, 2(uLogL - rLogL); `waldtest` from the unrestricted estimates alone, the restrictions' values r, their Jacobian R and the estimates' covariance; `lmtest` from the restricted model alone, its score and covariance. Each statistic is chi-square with as many degrees of freedom as restrictions.
syntax: [h, pValue, stat, cValue] = lratiotest(uLogL, rLogL, dof, alpha)
[h, pValue, stat, cValue] = waldtest(r, R, EstCov, alpha)
[h, pValue, stat, cValue] = lmtest(score, ParamCov, dof, alpha)

pages.summary: The Hodrick-Prescott trend of a series, and its cycle.
body: The trend is the smooth series that minimizes the squared distance to the data plus `smoothing` times its squared second differences (1600, for quarterly data, unless given; larger is smoother); the cycle is what is left. Each column is a series. Without outputs, the series and their trends are drawn.
syntax: With a smoothing of one's own.

examples.title: A trend through a cycle

body: Each lag shifts every series down by that many steps (a negative lag is a lead, shifting up), NaN where there is no value. The columns are every series at the first lag, then every series at the next.
